The lecture does one thing: it takes the oldest model in statistics and shows you three ways to fit it — one iterative algorithm that scales, one noisy variant of that algorithm that scales further, and one closed-form formula that needs no iteration at all. The reason to care is not linear regression. It is that every supervised learning algorithm in the rest of the course is assembled from these same four parts, and this is the only lecture where all four are simple enough to see at once.

PartIn this lectureLater in the course

losssquared errorlog-loss, hinge loss, cross-entropy
optimiserGD / SGD / closed formNewton’s method, SMO, Adam
justificationGaussian-noise MLEevery GLM, every generative model

Swap one part, keep the other three, and you have a different algorithm. That is the actual content of the lecture, and it is worth holding onto while the algebra goes past.

01 Setup and notation

The half of the lecture that looks like bookkeeping, and quietly decides how readable the next ten weeks are.

Supervised learning starts with a training set of mm labelled examples

{(x(i),y(i))}i=1m,x(i)∈ℝn+1,y(i)∈ℝ.\{(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{m},\qquad x^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1},\quad y^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}.

The superscript in parentheses is an index, never a power. A learning algorithm consumes this set and returns a function h:𝒳→𝒴h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} called the hypothesis; you then apply hh to inputs you have never seen.

SymbolMeaningWatch out

nnnumber of features, excluding the interceptso θ∈ℝn+1\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}
xj(i)x^{(i)}_jfeature jj of example iiexample index up top, feature index down low
x0=1x_0=1the intercept dummya convention, not data
θ\thetaparameters / weightswhat the algorithm learns
XXdesign matrix, m×(n+1)m\times(n+1)row ii is (x(i))⊤(x^{(i)})^\top
y→\vec{y}target vector, m×1m\times 1—
α\alphalearning ratethe only knob in the algorithm
Gap G1 — a notation trap the lecture cannot warn you about

The 2018 lecture uses mm for examples and nn for features. The current CS229 course notes (Ma & Ng) use nn for the number of examples and dd for the number of features. If you watch the video with the current PDF open, every single dimension argument will look wrong. Pick one convention and convert on sight; this page uses the lecture’s (mm examples, nn features) throughout.

The hypothesis, and what “linear” actually restricts

hθ(x)=θ0+θ1x1+…+θnxn=∑j=0nθjxj=θ⊤x.h_\theta(x)=\theta_0+\theta_1x_1+\dots+\theta_nx_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\theta_jx_j=\theta^\top x .

Setting x0=1x_0=1 is not a trick for tidiness; it is what lets the intercept be updated by exactly the same rule as every other weight, which is why no derivation below ever needs a special case for θ0\theta_0.

The single most misread word in the lecture

“Linear” means linear in θ\theta, not linear in xx. hθ(x)=θ0+θ1x+θ2x2+θ3logxh_\theta(x)=\theta_0+\theta_1x+\theta_2x^2+\theta_3\log x is still linear regression — it is a linear combination of fixed functions of the input. Everything on this page, including the closed-form solution, applies to it unchanged. What linearity actually forbids is things like θ1xθ2\theta_1x^{\theta_2}.

02 The cost function

Two lines of definition, and four separate reasons behind them that the lecture states as one.

J(θ)=12∑i=1m(hθ(x(i))−y(i))2=12∥Xθ−y→∥22.J(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\bigr)^2 =\tfrac12\lVert X\theta-\vec y\rVert_2^2 .

Minimising JJ over θ\theta is ordinary least squares. Every remaining section of this page is either a way to perform that minimisation or a reason to believe it is the right one.

Why squared, and not something else

  1. It is differentiable everywhere. |e||e| has a corner at 00; every gradient method below would need subgradients.
  2. It is convex — so a stationary point is a global minimum (proved in §3).
  3. It is quadratic, so setting the gradient to zero gives a linear system, which is why a closed form exists at all (§6).
  4. It is the maximum-likelihood loss when the noise is Gaussian (§8) — the lecture promises this and defers it.
Gap G2 — the 12\tfrac12, and the missing 1m\tfrac1m

The 12\tfrac12 is pure cosmetics: it cancels the 22 from differentiating the square. Rescaling JJ by any positive constant leaves argminθJ\arg\min_\theta J untouched, so it changes nothing about the answer.

The absence of 1m\tfrac1m is not cosmetic, and it bites in practice. With Ng’s sum convention, ∇J\nabla J grows linearly with mm, so a learning rate tuned on 100 examples is roughly 1000×1000\times too large on 100,000 examples and the run explodes. Many textbooks and every deep-learning framework therefore use the mean 12m∑(⋅)2\tfrac1{2m}\sum(\cdot)^2, which makes α\alpha roughly transferable across dataset sizes. Both are correct; you must know which one you are reading, because every α\alpha in this page is quoted for the sum convention.

Gap G3 — the price of squaring, which the lecture never mentions

Squaring means a residual of 10 counts a hundred times a residual of 1. Least squares therefore has a breakdown point of zero: one badly corrupted example, moved far enough, can drag the fit anywhere it likes. This is not a small-print caveat; it is the single most common reason a linear regression in the wild looks wrong. Robust alternatives — least absolute deviations, Huber loss — trade the closed form and some efficiency for immunity to it.

03 Gradient descent and the LMS rule

Start anywhere, repeatedly step downhill. The derivation is four lines; the two claims smuggled inside it take a page each.

θj:=θj−α∂∂θjJ(θ)simultaneously for all j=0,…,n.\theta_j := \theta_j-\alpha\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}J(\theta) \qquad\text{simultaneously for all }j=0,\dots,n.

Simultaneously matters. If you overwrite θ0\theta_0 and then use the new value while computing the update for θ1\theta_1, you are running a different algorithm (coordinate descent). It often still works, which is what makes the bug hard to find.

Deriving the partial derivative

Take one training example (x,y)(x,y) first, so the sum disappears:

  1. ∂∂θj12(hθ(x)−y)2=2⋅12(hθ(x)−y)⋅∂∂θj(hθ(x)−y)\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\;\tfrac12\bigl(h_\theta(x)-y\bigr)^2 = 2\cdot\tfrac12\bigl(h_\theta(x)-y\bigr)\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\bigl(h_\theta(x)-y\bigr)

    by the chain rule — and this is exactly where the 12\tfrac12 earns its keep.

  2. ∂∂θj(hθ(x)−y)=∂∂θj(∑k=0nθkxk−y)=xj\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\bigl(h_\theta(x)-y\bigr) =\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\bigl(\sum_{k=0}^{n}\theta_kx_k-y\bigr)=x_j

    because every term with k≠jk\ne j is constant in θj\theta_j, and yy does not depend on θ\theta at all.

  3. ∂∂θjJ(θ)=(hθ(x)−y)xj\boxed{\;\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}J(\theta)=\bigl(h_\theta(x)-y\bigr)x_j\;}

    Read it as a sentence: error × the input that caused it. That product is the entire content of the update, and it reappears verbatim in logistic regression, in the perceptron, and in backpropagation.

  4. Summing over the training set gives the full gradient ∂J∂θj=∑i=1m(hθ(x(i))−y(i))xj(i),∇θJ=X⊤(Xθ−y→).\frac{\partial J}{\partial\theta_j}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\bigr)x^{(i)}_j, \qquad \nabla_\theta J=X^\top(X\theta-\vec y).

Substituting into the update gives the LMS (least mean squares, or Widrow–Hoff) rule:

θj:=θj+α∑i=1m(y(i)−hθ(x(i)))xj(i)⇔θ:=θ−αX⊤(Xθ−y→).\theta_j:=\theta_j+\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl(y^{(i)}-h_\theta(x^{(i)})\bigr)x^{(i)}_j \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \theta:=\theta-\alpha X^\top(X\theta-\vec y).

Note the sign flip: writing the residual as y−hy-h instead of h−yh-y turns the minus into a plus. Both forms appear in the literature and they are the same algorithm. Three properties fall straight out of the rule:

  • the step is proportional to the error, so it shrinks automatically as the fit improves — no schedule needed to slow down near the optimum;
  • a feature that is zero on an example contributes nothing to that example’s update;
  • a feature measured on a large numeric scale produces large steps in its own coordinate — the seed of the scaling problem in §4.
Algorithm 1   Batch gradient descent
  1. initialise θ←0\theta\leftarrow 0 (any point works — JJ is convex)
  2. repeat until a stopping rule fires:
  3. g←X⊤(Xθ−y→)g\leftarrow X^\top(X\theta-\vec y) # one sweep over all m examples
  4. θ←θ−αg\theta\leftarrow\theta-\alpha g
  5. return θ\theta

“Batch” is a historical name meaning the whole batch of data per step. In modern deep-learning usage “batch” means a small subset, which is the exact opposite. Read the era, not the word.

Gap G4 — why the gradient, specifically?

The lecture says the gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent. Here is the one-line proof. The change in JJ from a small step δu\delta u with ∥u∥=1\lVert u\rVert=1 is J(θ+δu)−J(θ)≈δ∇J⊤uJ(\theta+\delta u)-J(\theta)\approx\delta\,\nabla J^\top u. By Cauchy–Schwarz, |∇J⊤u|≤∥∇J∥|\nabla J^\top u|\le\lVert\nabla J\rVert, with equality exactly when u=±∇J/∥∇J∥u=\pm\nabla J/\lVert\nabla J\rVert. So among all unit directions, −∇J-\nabla J is the one that decreases JJ fastest.

The catch, and it is the reason Newton’s method exists: steepest is defined with respect to the Euclidean norm, which is an arbitrary choice. If the coordinates have wildly different scales, “steepest in Euclidean distance” is not the direction that actually reaches the minimum soonest. That is precisely what Fig 5 shows.

Gap G5 — is JJ really convex? (the bowl, proved)

The lecture draws a bowl and moves on. The proof is short. Differentiating ∇J=X⊤(Xθ−y→)\nabla J=X^\top(X\theta-\vec y) once more gives a constant Hessian

∇2J=X⊤X.\nabla^2 J=X^\top X.

For any v∈ℝn+1v\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, v⊤X⊤Xv=∥Xv∥2≥0v^\top X^\top Xv=\lVert Xv\rVert^2\ge0, so X⊤X≽0X^\top X\succeq0 and JJ is convex. Therefore every stationary point is a global minimum and there are no local traps — the single fact that makes both gradient descent and the normal equations legitimate.

Strict convexity (and hence a unique minimiser) needs ∥Xv∥2>0\lVert Xv\rVert^2>0 for all v≠0v\ne0, i.e. XX has full column rank. When it does not, the bowl has a flat valley floor: infinitely many θ\theta achieve the same minimum JJ. Hold on to this; it is the whole of §7.

04 The learning rate — the part the lecture waves at

“Too small is slow, too large diverges” is true and unusable. For least squares you can write the exact threshold down.

Write H=X⊤XH=X^\top X and let θ⋆\theta^\star be a minimiser. Subtracting ∇J(θ⋆)=0\nabla J(\theta^\star)=0 from the update turns it into a pure linear recursion in the error ek=θk−θ⋆e_k=\theta_k-\theta^\star:

θk+1=θk−αH(θk−θ⋆)⇒ek+1=(I−αH)ek⇒ek=(I−αH)ke0.\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\alpha H(\theta_k-\theta^\star) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e_{k+1}=(I-\alpha H)\,e_k \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e_k=(I-\alpha H)^k e_0 .

Decompose e0e_0 in the eigenbasis of HH. The component along the eigenvector with eigenvalue λ\lambda is multiplied by (1−αλ)(1-\alpha\lambda) every iteration. So the run converges if and only if |1−αλ|<1|1-\alpha\lambda|<1 for every eigenvalue, which is

0<α<2λmax(X⊤X)\boxed{\;0<\alpha<\frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}(X^\top X)}\;}

and the slowest-decaying component sets the rate:

∥ek∥≤ρk∥e0∥,ρ=max(|1−αλmin|,|1−αλmax|).\lVert e_k\rVert\le\rho^k\lVert e_0\rVert,\qquad \rho=\max\bigl(|1-\alpha\lambda_{\min}|,\,|1-\alpha\lambda_{\max}|\bigr).

Minimising ρ\rho over α\alpha gives the best possible step, α⋆=2λmin+λmax\alpha^\star=\dfrac{2}{\lambda_{\min}+\lambda_{\max}}, at which

ρ⋆=κ−1κ+1,κ=λmaxλmin=condition number of X⊤X.\rho^\star=\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1},\qquad \kappa=\frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}=\text{condition number of }X^\top X .

This is the whole story of gradient descent in one number. κ=1\kappa=1 (circular contours) converges in a single step. κ=100\kappa=100 needs roughly κ2ln(1/ε)≈350\tfrac{\kappa}{2}\ln(1/\varepsilon)\approx 350 iterations for three digits. κ=106\kappa=10^6 — entirely normal for unscaled real-world features — is hopeless.

Gap G6 — feature scaling, absent from the lecture entirely

κ\kappa is not a property of the problem. It is a property of the units you chose. A feature in square feet (∼103\sim10^3) sitting beside a feature in bedrooms (∼100\sim10^0) makes X⊤XX^\top X badly conditioned before you have written a line of code. Standardising each feature,

zj=xj−μjσj(μj,σjcomputed on the TRAINING set only),z_j=\frac{x_j-\mu_j}{\sigma_j}\qquad(\mu_j,\sigma_j\ \text{computed on the TRAINING set only}),

typically drops κ\kappa by orders of magnitude and costs one pass over the data. Two things that are easy to get wrong: fit μ,σ\mu,\sigma on the training split and reuse them on validation and test, otherwise you have leaked; and never scale the intercept column, whose σ\sigma is zero.

Scaling changes nothing about the fitted function — predictions and the optimal JJ are identical, and the recovered coefficients map back exactly by θjraw=θjscaled/σj\theta_j^{\text{raw}}=\theta_j^{\text{scaled}}/\sigma_j. It changes only how many iterations you spend getting there.

Gap G7 — “repeat until convergence” is not a stopping rule

Pick one and state it. In rough order of quality:

  • Gradient norm: stop when ∥∇J∥≤ε\lVert\nabla J\rVert\le\varepsilon. Scale-aware and closest to the real condition ∇J=0\nabla J=0.
  • Relative parameter change: ∥θk+1−θk∥≤ε(1+∥θk∥)\lVert\theta_{k+1}-\theta_k\rVert\le\varepsilon(1+\lVert\theta_k\rVert).
  • Relative loss change: |Jk−Jk+1|≤ε|Jk||J_k-J_{k+1}|\le\varepsilon|J_k|. Popular, but it also fires when α\alpha is far too small — slow is not the same as done.
  • Held-out loss stops improving (early stopping). The only one of the four that is about the thing you actually care about, and it doubles as regularisation.
  • Always cap the iteration count as well, so a diverging run terminates.

05 Stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent

One pass of batch GD over a billion examples costs a billion evaluations and produces a single update. Stochastic gradient descent refuses to wait.

Algorithm 2   Stochastic gradient descent
  1. initialise θ←0\theta\leftarrow0
  2. repeat for each epoch:
  3. shuffle the training set
  4. for i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m:
  5.    θ←θ−α(hθ(x(i))−y(i))x(i)\theta\leftarrow\theta-\alpha\bigl(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\bigr)x^{(i)}
  6. return θ\theta

Same expression, different scope: batch GD sums the per-example gradient over all mm examples before moving; SGD moves on each one. Mini-batch interpolates, using a subset of size bb (typically 32–512), and is what essentially everything actually runs.

Gap G8 — why does following a wrong gradient work at all?

Because it is wrong only in variance, not in expectation. Sample ii uniformly from {1,…,m}\{1,\dots,m\} and let gi=(hθ(x(i))−y(i))x(i)g_i=(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)})x^{(i)}. Then

𝔼i[gi]=1m∑i=1m(hθ(x(i))−y(i))x(i)=1m∇J(θ).\mathbb{E}_i[g_i]=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)}\bigr)x^{(i)} =\frac1m\nabla J(\theta).

The stochastic step is an unbiased estimate of the true gradient, scaled by 1/m1/m. SGD is therefore a random walk whose drift is exactly downhill; the noise averages out over many steps. That is the entire justification, and it is worth remembering that it is a statement about the average, not about any single step — individual SGD steps routinely increase JJ.

A mini-batch of size bb averages bb independent such estimates, so its variance falls like 1/b1/b: the gradient gets b\sqrt{b} times cleaner for bb times the work. That sub-linear return is exactly why nobody uses b=mb=m, and why bb is usually chosen by what keeps the hardware busy rather than by statistics.

Gap G9 — SGD with a constant step never converges

The lecture notes that SGD “oscillates” near the minimum. It is worth being precise: with a fixed α\alpha, SGD does not converge to θ⋆\theta^\star. It converges in distribution to a stationary cloud whose radius scales like ασ2\alpha\sigma^2 — a noise ball. Running longer does not shrink it.

To actually converge you must decay the step size. The Robbins–Monro conditions are

∑k=1∞αk=∞(you can still travel any distance),∑k=1∞αk2<∞(the noise is summable),\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\quad\text{(you can still travel any distance)}, \qquad\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha_k^2<\infty\quad\text{(the noise is summable)},

satisfied by αk=α0/(1+k/t0)\alpha_k=\alpha_0/(1+k/t_0) and by αk=α0k−p\alpha_k=\alpha_0k^{-p} for p∈(12,1]p\in(\tfrac12,1]. Note that αk=α0/k\alpha_k=\alpha_0/\sqrt{k} fails the second condition and is used anyway when you only want to get close quickly. The practical recipe: constant α\alpha until progress stalls, then decay.

Gap G10 — shuffle, and shuffle again

If the file is sorted by label, or by date, or by anything at all correlated with yy, sequential SGD will spend a whole epoch being pulled in one direction and then an epoch being pulled back. Reshuffle every epoch, not once at the start. In practice random reshuffling (sampling without replacement) also converges somewhat faster than sampling with replacement, even though the clean unbiasedness argument in G8 is the with-replacement one.

Gap G11 — what the last decade added

Plain SGD is a starting point, not the state of the art. Everything below is the same update with an extra term, and each addresses a defect visible in the figures above:

  • Momentum v←βv+∇J,θ←θ−αvv\leftarrow\beta v+\nabla J,\;\theta\leftarrow\theta-\alpha v: accumulates a velocity, which cancels the zig-zag in Fig 5 and effectively improves the κ\kappa dependence from κ\kappa to κ\sqrt{\kappa}.
  • AdaGrad / RMSProp: divide each coordinate’s step by the running root-mean-square of its own past gradients — an automatic, online version of the feature scaling in G6.
  • Adam: momentum and RMSProp together, plus bias correction. The default optimiser in most deep-learning code.
  • Newton’s method θ←θ−H−1∇J\theta\leftarrow\theta-H^{-1}\nabla J: for least squares H=X⊤XH=X^\top X is constant, so one Newton step lands exactly on θ⋆\theta^\star — that step is the normal equations. CS229 returns to this when fitting logistic regression.

06 The normal equations

JJ is a quadratic, so ∇J=0\nabla J=0 is a linear system. Solve it and you are done — no learning rate, no iterations, no convergence to argue about.

Stack the examples into the design matrix and target vector

X=[(x(1))⊤⋮(x(m))⊤]∈ℝm×(n+1),y→=[y(1)⋮y(m)],Xθ−y→=[hθ(x(1))−y(1)⋮hθ(x(m))−y(m)].X=\begin{bmatrix}(x^{(1)})^\top\\ \vdots\\ (x^{(m)})^\top\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times(n+1)}, \qquad \vec y=\begin{bmatrix}y^{(1)}\\ \vdots\\ y^{(m)}\end{bmatrix}, \qquad X\theta-\vec y=\begin{bmatrix}h_\theta(x^{(1)})-y^{(1)}\\ \vdots\\ h_\theta(x^{(m)})-y^{(m)}\end{bmatrix}.

Since z⊤z=∑kzk2z^\top z=\sum_k z_k^2, the cost is just

J(θ)=12(Xθ−y→)⊤(Xθ−y→).J(\theta)=\tfrac12(X\theta-\vec y)^\top(X\theta-\vec y).
Gap G12 — the matrix calculus, without the trace identities

The lecture reaches for ∇Atr(ABA⊤C)\nabla_A\operatorname{tr}(ABA^\top C) and friends, which is elegant if you already know them and mystifying if you do not. You never need them here. Expand the quadratic like a scalar and differentiate term by term.

Derivation, by expansion

  1. Multiply out, using θ⊤X⊤y→=y→⊤Xθ\theta^\top X^\top\vec y=\vec y^\top X\theta (a scalar equals its own transpose):

    J(θ)=12(θ⊤X⊤Xθ−2y→⊤Xθ+y→⊤y→).J(\theta)=\tfrac12\bigl(\theta^\top X^\top X\theta-2\,\vec y^\top X\theta+\vec y^\top\vec y\bigr).

  2. Apply two rules, both provable in one line by writing out the sums:

    ∇θ(b⊤θ)=b,∇θ(θ⊤Aθ)=2Aθfor symmetric A.\nabla_\theta\,(b^\top\theta)=b,\qquad \nabla_\theta\,(\theta^\top A\theta)=2A\theta\ \ \text{for symmetric }A.

    Here A=X⊤XA=X^\top X is symmetric because (X⊤X)⊤=X⊤X(X^\top X)^\top=X^\top X, and b⊤=y→⊤Xb^\top=\vec y^\top X.

  3. ∇θJ=12(2X⊤Xθ−2X⊤y→)=X⊤Xθ−X⊤y→=X⊤(Xθ−y→),\nabla_\theta J=\tfrac12\bigl(2X^\top X\theta-2X^\top\vec y\bigr)=X^\top X\theta-X^\top\vec y = X^\top(X\theta-\vec y),

    which is the same gradient the LMS derivation produced, as it must be.

  4. Set it to zero. Because JJ is convex (G5), this stationary point is a global minimum, not merely a critical point:

    X⊤Xθ=X⊤y→(the normal equations)X^\top X\,\theta = X^\top\vec y \qquad\text{(the normal equations)}

    and when X⊤XX^\top X is invertible,

    θ⋆=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y→\boxed{\;\theta^\star=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\vec y\;}

Why they are called normal

Read the stationarity condition as it is written:

X⊤(Xθ−y→)=0⇔the residual is orthogonal to every column of X.X^\top(X\theta-\vec y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{the residual is orthogonal to every column of }X.

The set {Xθ:θ∈ℝn+1}\{X\theta:\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\} is the column space of XX — every prediction the model is capable of producing. Least squares picks the point in that subspace closest to y→\vec y, which is its orthogonal projection. “Normal” here means perpendicular. Two consequences you can check on any fitted model:

  • ŷ=X(X⊤X)−1X⊤y→=Py→\hat y=X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\vec y=P\vec y, where PP is a projection matrix: P2=PP^2=P and P⊤=PP^\top=P. Projecting twice does nothing new.
  • Because the intercept contributes an all-ones column, orthogonality to it says ∑i(hθ(x(i))−y(i))=0\sum_i(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)})=0: the residuals of any least-squares fit with an intercept sum to exactly zero. A quick and genuinely useful sanity check on your code.

07 When the closed form breaks — and which method to pick

The formula assumes an inverse exists. Three separate things can go wrong, and each has a different fix.

1. X⊤XX^\top X is singular

X⊤XX^\top X is invertible exactly when XX has full column rank, i.e. rank(X)=n+1\operatorname{rank}(X)=n+1. It fails in two ways:

  • Redundant features. Some column is a linear combination of others — size in square feet and size in square metres, or a set of one-hot dummies that includes every level and an intercept (the “dummy variable trap”). Drop the redundancy.
  • More features than examples (m<n+1m<n+1). Then rank(X)≤m<n+1\operatorname{rank}(X)\le m<n+1 always, whatever the data. Get more data, reduce features, or regularise.

In both cases the minimiser is not unique: there is a whole affine subspace of θ\theta achieving the same minimal JJ. The normal equations X⊤Xθ=X⊤y→X^\top X\theta=X^\top\vec y are still consistent — they always have at least one solution — you simply cannot get it by inverting. Two standard resolutions:

  • Pseudoinverse: θ=X+y→\theta=X^{+}\vec y picks the minimum-norm member of that solution set. This is what numpy.linalg.lstsq and pinv return, which is why they succeed on inputs that make inv raise.
  • Ridge regression: minimise J(θ)+λ2∥θ1:n∥2J(\theta)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\theta_{1:n}\rVert^2, giving
θridge=(X⊤X+λD)−1X⊤y→,D=diag(0,1,…,1).\theta_{\text{ridge}}=(X^\top X+\lambda D)^{-1}X^\top\vec y, \qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\dots,1).

For λ>0\lambda>0, v⊤(X⊤X+λI)v=∥Xv∥2+λ∥v∥2>0v^\top(X^\top X+\lambda I)v=\lVert Xv\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert v\rVert^2>0 for every v≠0v\ne0, so the matrix is strictly positive definite and always invertible — even when m<nm<n. The zero in DD leaves the intercept unpenalised; shrinking it would make the fit depend on where you happen to put the origin of yy.

Gap G13 — near-singular is the dangerous case, not singular

Exact singularity throws an exception and you notice. Near singularity returns a confident answer that is garbage: coefficients with huge magnitudes and opposite signs, which flip when you resample the data. Warning signs are a large κ(X⊤X)\kappa(X^\top X), coefficients far outside the plausible range of the response, and standard errors much larger than the estimates. Check κ\kappa before you interpret a single coefficient.

2. You computed the inverse

Gap G14 — write (X⊤X)−1X⊤y→(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\vec y, never compute it

Forming X⊤XX^\top X squares the condition number: κ(X⊤X)=κ(X)2\kappa(X^\top X)=\kappa(X)^2. A design matrix with κ(X)=108\kappa(X)=10^{8} — perfectly ordinary — produces a normal-equation system with κ=1016\kappa=10^{16}, which is the entire precision of a float64. You lose the answer to rounding.

  • np.linalg.inv(X.T@X)@X.T@y — the textbook formula, the worst option.
  • np.linalg.solve(X.T@X, X.T@y) — Cholesky, roughly twice as fast and more stable, but still at κ(X)2\kappa(X)^2.
  • np.linalg.lstsq(X, y) — QR or SVD applied to XX itself, so it works at κ(X)\kappa(X), and it returns the minimum-norm solution instead of failing when XX is rank deficient. Use this one.

The boxed formula is a statement about mathematics. It is not an instruction to your linear algebra library.

3. The matrix is simply too big

MethodCostMemoryHyper­parametersUse it when
Normal equationsO(mn² + n³), onceneeds all of XXnonen≲104n\lesssim10^4 and the data fits in memory
Batch GDO(kmn)all of XX per stepα\alpha, stopping rulenn large, mm moderate, or XX is sparse
SGD / mini-batchO(kbn)one batchα\alpha, schedule, bbmm huge, streaming data, or online updates

The n3n^3 term is what rules the closed form out: at n=104n=10^4 it is already 101210^{12} operations, and it grows by a factor of a thousand for every factor of ten in nn. Gradient descent is linear in nn, which is the whole reason it survives into the rest of the course — nothing after this lecture has a closed form at all.

08 Why squared error, finally

The lecture promises a probabilistic justification and moves on. Here it is; it takes six lines and it is the template for every model in the course.

Assume: the targets are generated by a true linear function plus noise,

y(i)=θ⊤x(i)+ε(i),ε(i)∼iid𝒩(0,σ2).y^{(i)}=\theta^\top x^{(i)}+\varepsilon^{(i)},\qquad \varepsilon^{(i)}\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).

The Gaussian is not arbitrary: by the central limit theorem, noise that is the sum of many small independent effects is approximately Gaussian, and it is the maximum-entropy distribution for a fixed variance — the least-committal choice you can make.

  1. The assumption is exactly the statement

    p(y(i)∣x(i);θ)=12πσexp(−(y(i)−θ⊤x(i))22σ2).p(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(y^{(i)}-\theta^\top x^{(i)})^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).

    The semicolon matters: θ\theta is a fixed unknown constant we are parameterised by, not a random variable we condition on. That is the frequentist reading.

  2. Independence across examples makes the likelihood a product:

    L(θ)=∏i=1mp(y(i)∣x(i);θ).L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}p(y^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)};\theta).

  3. Take logs, which is monotone so the maximiser is unchanged:

    ℓ(θ)=mlog12πσ−1σ2⋅12∑i=1m(y(i)−θ⊤x(i))2.\ell(\theta)=m\log\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} -\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\cdot\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl(y^{(i)}-\theta^\top x^{(i)}\bigr)^2 .

  4. The first term is constant in θ\theta and 1/σ21/\sigma^2 is a positive constant, so

    argmaxθℓ(θ)=argminθ12∑i(θ⊤x(i)−y(i))2=argminθJ(θ).\arg\max_\theta\ \ell(\theta)\;=\;\arg\min_\theta\ \tfrac12\sum_i\bigl(\theta^\top x^{(i)}-y^{(i)}\bigr)^2 \;=\;\arg\min_\theta\ J(\theta).

    Least squares is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise. The cost function was never arbitrary.

Three things worth noticing
  • σ\sigma cancels out. The MLE for θ\theta does not depend on the noise level at all — which is why you never have to estimate σ\sigma before fitting. (Its own MLE, if you want it, is σ̂2=1m∥Xθ̂−y→∥2\hat\sigma^2=\tfrac1m\lVert X\hat\theta-\vec y\rVert^2.)
  • Change the noise distribution and you change the loss. Laplace noise gives least absolute deviations; Bernoulli gives logistic regression’s log-loss. This single recipe generates most of the losses in the course.
  • Add a Gaussian prior on θ\theta and maximise the posterior instead of the likelihood, and you get ridge regression exactly. Regularisation is a prior.
Gap G15 — and where the assumptions fail

The derivation buys you least squares only if you accept four things, each of which fails routinely on real data:

  • Independence. Time series, repeated measures on the same subject, and clustered samples all violate it. Errors are correlated; standard errors come out far too small and you become confident about nothing.
  • Constant variance (homoscedasticity). If the spread of yy grows with xx — extremely common with prices, counts, incomes — the correct estimator is weighted least squares, which weights each example by 1/σi21/\sigma_i^2.
  • Gaussianity. Heavy tails make least squares inefficient and fragile (see G3).
  • Correct mean function. If 𝔼[y∣x]\mathbb{E}[y\mid x] is not linear in your features, no amount of data fixes it — you are fitting the wrong model class.

Diagnosis costs one plot: residuals against fitted values. Structure in that plot — a curve, a fan, a trend — means one of the four has failed.

09 What the lecture does not mention at all

Everything above is about minimising JJ on the training set. Nothing above says that is the right thing to want.

Gap G16 — the model class is a choice, and it is yours

Because linear regression is linear in θ\theta and not in xx (§1), you may feed it any fixed transformation of the input: x2x^2, logx\log x, x1x2x_1x_2, a spline basis. Every formula on this page carries over verbatim. That freedom is the point — and it is also the trap, because a rich enough basis can drive JJ to exactly zero while predicting nothing.

Gap G17 — the minimum you should add before using any of this
  • Split the data before you look at it: train / validation / test, or kk-fold cross-validation when mm is small. Every hyperparameter — α\alpha, λ\lambda, the polynomial degree — is chosen on validation, and the test set is touched exactly once.
  • Report a scale-free score alongside JJ: R2=1−∑i(y(i)−ŷ(i))2∑i(y(i)−y‾)2R^2=1-\dfrac{\sum_i(y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)})^2}{\sum_i(y^{(i)}-\bar y)^2}, which is the fraction of variance explained. R2=0R^2=0 means you have matched the constant predictor y‾\bar y; negative means you have done worse than it.
  • Regularise when features outnumber examples or are correlated: ridge (L2L_2) shrinks smoothly and keeps the closed form, lasso (L1L_1) sets coefficients exactly to zero and needs an iterative solver.
  • Plot the residuals against fitted values. Ten seconds, and it catches nonlinearity, heteroscedasticity and outliers at once.

13 Problems

Work them before opening the solutions. Difficulty in stars; the four-star ones are the ones worth the fight.

Problem 1 ★★

Starting from J(θ)=12∑i=1m(θ⊤x(i)−y(i))2J(\theta)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m(\theta^\top x^{(i)}-y^{(i)})^2, derive ∂J/∂θj\partial J/\partial\theta_j for general mm, and then write the result in matrix form.

Solution

Differentiation is linear, so differentiate term by term. For term ii, the chain rule gives 2⋅12(θ⊤x(i)−y(i))⋅∂θj(θ⊤x(i)−y(i))2\cdot\tfrac12(\theta^\top x^{(i)}-y^{(i)})\cdot\partial_{\theta_j}(\theta^\top x^{(i)}-y^{(i)}), and ∂θj∑kθkxk(i)=xj(i)\partial_{\theta_j}\sum_k\theta_kx^{(i)}_k=x^{(i)}_j. Hence

∂J∂θj=∑i=1m(θ⊤x(i)−y(i))xj(i).\frac{\partial J}{\partial\theta_j}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl(\theta^\top x^{(i)}-y^{(i)}\bigr)x^{(i)}_j .

The inner sum is the jj-th entry of X⊤rX^\top r with r=Xθ−y→r=X\theta-\vec y, because the jj-th row of X⊤X^\top is the jj-th feature across all examples. So ∇θJ=X⊤(Xθ−y→)\nabla_\theta J=X^\top(X\theta-\vec y).

Problem 2 ★★

Prove JJ is convex, and state exactly when it is strictly convex.

Solution

∇2J=X⊤X\nabla^2J=X^\top X, independent of θ\theta. For any vv, v⊤X⊤Xv=(Xv)⊤(Xv)=∥Xv∥2≥0v^\top X^\top Xv=(Xv)^\top(Xv)=\lVert Xv\rVert^2\ge0, so the Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere and JJ is convex.

Strict convexity requires ∥Xv∥2>0\lVert Xv\rVert^2>0 for all v≠0v\ne0, i.e. Xv=0⇒v=0Xv=0\Rightarrow v=0, i.e. XX has full column rank n+1n+1. Since rank(X)≤min(m,n+1)\operatorname{rank}(X)\le\min(m,n+1), a necessary condition is m≥n+1m\ge n+1: you need at least as many examples as parameters.

Problem 3 ★★

Show that if the design matrix contains an all-ones intercept column, the residuals at the least-squares optimum sum to exactly zero. Why is this a useful unit test?

Solution

At the optimum X⊤(Xθ⋆−y→)=0X^\top(X\theta^\star-\vec y)=0, so the residual vector rr is orthogonal to every column of XX. Taking the inner product with the all-ones column, 𝟏⊤r=∑iri=0\mathbf{1}^\top r=\sum_i r_i=0.

It is a useful test because it is an exact algebraic identity, not an approximation: any implementation that reports a non-negligible residual sum has either failed to converge, dropped the intercept column, or has a bug. It also implies the fitted line passes through (x‾,y‾)(\bar x,\bar y).

Problem 4 ★★★★

Let H=X⊤XH=X^\top X be invertible with eigenvalues λ1≤…≤λn+1\lambda_1\le\dots\le\lambda_{n+1}. Show θk−θ⋆=(I−αH)k(θ0−θ⋆)\theta_{k}-\theta^\star=(I-\alpha H)^k(\theta_0-\theta^\star), derive the exact condition on α\alpha for convergence, and find the α\alpha that converges fastest.

Solution

The update is θk+1=θk−α(Hθk−X⊤y→)\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\alpha(H\theta_k-X^\top\vec y). Optimality gives X⊤y→=Hθ⋆X^\top\vec y=H\theta^\star, so θk+1=θk−αH(θk−θ⋆)\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\alpha H(\theta_k-\theta^\star). Subtract θ⋆\theta^\star from both sides: ek+1=(I−αH)eke_{k+1}=(I-\alpha H)e_k, and induction gives ek=(I−αH)ke0e_k=(I-\alpha H)^ke_0.

HH is symmetric, so write H=QΛQ⊤H=Q\Lambda Q^\top; then (I−αH)k=Q(I−αΛ)kQ⊤(I-\alpha H)^k=Q(I-\alpha\Lambda)^kQ^\top, and the ii-th coordinate of the error in the eigenbasis is multiplied by (1−αλi)k(1-\alpha\lambda_i)^k. This tends to zero for every ii iff |1−αλi|<1|1-\alpha\lambda_i|<1 for every ii, i.e. 0<α<2/λmax0<\alpha<2/\lambda_{\max}.

The convergence factor is ρ(α)=maxi|1−αλi|=max(|1−αλmin|,|1−αλmax|)\rho(\alpha)=\max_i|1-\alpha\lambda_i| =\max(|1-\alpha\lambda_{\min}|,|1-\alpha\lambda_{\max}|), a piecewise-linear V in α\alpha: decreasing while 1−αλmin1-\alpha\lambda_{\min} dominates, increasing once αλmax−1\alpha\lambda_{\max}-1 does. The minimum is where they cross, 1−αλmin=αλmax−11-\alpha\lambda_{\min}=\alpha\lambda_{\max}-1, giving α⋆=2/(λmin+λmax)\alpha^\star=2/(\lambda_{\min}+\lambda_{\max}) and ρ⋆=(κ−1)/(κ+1)\rho^\star=(\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1).

Problem 5 ★★★

Replace XX by X̃=XS\tilde X=XS for an invertible diagonal SS (i.e. rescale each feature). How do θ⋆\theta^\star, the fitted predictions, J(θ⋆)J(\theta^\star), and κ(X⊤X)\kappa(X^\top X) change?

Solution

θ̃⋆=(S⊤X⊤XS)−1S⊤X⊤y→=S−1(X⊤X)−1X⊤y→=S−1θ⋆\tilde\theta^\star=(S^\top X^\top XS)^{-1}S^\top X^\top\vec y =S^{-1}(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\vec y=S^{-1}\theta^\star.

Predictions are unchanged: X̃θ̃⋆=XSS−1θ⋆=Xθ⋆\tilde X\tilde\theta^\star=XSS^{-1}\theta^\star=X\theta^\star. Therefore JJ at the optimum, the residuals, and R2R^2 are all unchanged — rescaling features cannot change what the model is, only how its coefficients are expressed.

κ\kappa does change, arbitrarily: X̃⊤X̃=S(X⊤X)S\tilde X^\top\tilde X=S(X^\top X)S, and by choosing SS you can make the condition number essentially anything you like. That is the whole content of G6 — conditioning is a property of your parameterisation, so it is yours to fix.

Problem 6 ★★★

You append a duplicate of an existing feature to XX. Show X⊤XX^\top X becomes singular, and describe the full set of minimisers of JJ.

Solution

Say columns pp and qq are equal. Let v=ep−eqv=e_p-e_q; then Xv=0Xv=0, so X⊤Xv=0X^\top Xv=0 and vv is a null vector: X⊤XX^\top X is singular and JJ is convex but not strictly so.

If θ⋆\theta^\star is any minimiser then X(θ⋆+cv)=Xθ⋆X(\theta^\star+cv)=X\theta^\star for every c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, so J(θ⋆+cv)=J(θ⋆)J(\theta^\star+cv)=J(\theta^\star). The solution set is the line θ⋆+span{v}\theta^\star+\operatorname{span}\{v\} — in general, the affine set θ⋆+𝒩(X)\theta^\star+\mathcal{N}(X). Predictions are identical for every member; only the coefficients differ, which is exactly why coefficients of collinear features are not interpretable. lstsq returns the member of smallest norm; ridge with λ>0\lambda>0 picks a unique point too, by splitting the weight evenly between the duplicates.

Problem 7 ★★

Sampling ii uniformly at random, show the SGD step direction is an unbiased estimate of ∇J\nabla J up to a constant, and state what that constant does to your choice of α\alpha.

Solution

𝔼i[gi]=∑i=1m1m(hθ(x(i))−y(i))x(i)=1m∇J\mathbb{E}_i[g_i]=\sum_{i=1}^m\tfrac1m(h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)})x^{(i)}=\tfrac1m\nabla J.

The constant is 1/m1/m. So an SGD step with rate α\alpha moves, in expectation, as far as a batch step with rate α/m\alpha/m; over one epoch of mm updates the total expected displacement matches one batch step of size α\alpha. Practically: a learning rate tuned for batch GD under the sum convention is roughly the right per-epoch budget, and you should not shrink it by mm again for SGD.

Problem 8 ★★★

Derive the ridge solution from Jλ(θ)=12∥Xθ−y→∥2+λ2∥θ∥2J_\lambda(\theta)=\tfrac12\lVert X\theta-\vec y\rVert^2 +\tfrac\lambda2\lVert\theta\rVert^2, and prove X⊤X+λIX^\top X+\lambda I is invertible for every λ>0\lambda>0, whatever XX is.

Solution

∇Jλ=X⊤(Xθ−y→)+λθ=(X⊤X+λI)θ−X⊤y→\nabla J_\lambda=X^\top(X\theta-\vec y)+\lambda\theta=(X^\top X+\lambda I)\theta-X^\top\vec y. Setting it to zero gives θ=(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y→\theta=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top\vec y.

For any v≠0v\ne0, v⊤(X⊤X+λI)v=∥Xv∥2+λ∥v∥2≥λ∥v∥2>0v^\top(X^\top X+\lambda I)v=\lVert Xv\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert v\rVert^2 \ge\lambda\lVert v\rVert^2>0. A symmetric matrix with strictly positive quadratic form is positive definite, hence has all eigenvalues ≥λ>0\ge\lambda>0 and is invertible. Note also κ(X⊤X+λI)≤(λmax+λ)/λ\kappa(X^\top X+\lambda I)\le(\lambda_{\max}+\lambda)/\lambda, which is bounded — ridge caps the conditioning as well as the coefficients.

Problem 9 ★★★

Some examples are more reliable than others. Minimise Jw(θ)=12∑iwi(θ⊤x(i)−y(i))2J_w(\theta)=\tfrac12\sum_i w_i(\theta^\top x^{(i)}-y^{(i)})^2 with wi>0w_i>0 and derive the weighted normal equations.

Solution

With W=diag(w1,…,wm)W=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,\dots,w_m), Jw=12(Xθ−y→)⊤W(Xθ−y→)J_w=\tfrac12(X\theta-\vec y)^\top W(X\theta-\vec y). Expanding and differentiating exactly as in §6 (using W⊤=WW^\top=W) gives ∇Jw=X⊤W(Xθ−y→)\nabla J_w=X^\top W(X\theta-\vec y), so

X⊤WXθ=X⊤Wy→,θ⋆=(X⊤WX)−1X⊤Wy→.X^\top WX\,\theta=X^\top W\vec y,\qquad \theta^\star=(X^\top WX)^{-1}X^\top W\vec y .

This is the right estimator when the noise variance differs by example: wi=1/σi2w_i=1/\sigma_i^2 recovers the MLE for heteroscedastic Gaussian noise (G15). Choosing wiw_i to depend on the distance from a query point instead gives locally weighted regression, the next algorithm in CS229.

Problem 10 ★★

Data: x=(1,2,3,4)x=(1,2,3,4), y=(2,3,5,4)y=(2,3,5,4), model hθ(x)=θ0+θ1xh_\theta(x)=\theta_0+\theta_1x. (a) Compute X⊤XX^\top X, X⊤y→X^\top\vec y and θ⋆\theta^\star by hand. (b) Compute J(θ⋆)J(\theta^\star). (c) Find the largest stable α\alpha. (d) Run two batch GD steps from θ=(0,0)\theta=(0,0) with α=0.05\alpha=0.05.

Solution

(a) X⊤X=[4101030]X^\top X=\begin{bmatrix}4&10\\10&30\end{bmatrix}, X⊤y→=[1439]X^\top\vec y=\begin{bmatrix}14\\39\end{bmatrix}. The determinant is 120−100=20120-100=20, so (X⊤X)−1=120[30−10−104](X^\top X)^{-1}=\tfrac1{20}\begin{bmatrix}30&-10\\-10&4\end{bmatrix} and θ⋆=120(30⋅14−10⋅39,−10⋅14+4⋅39)=120(30,16)=(1.5,0.8)\theta^\star=\tfrac1{20}(30\!\cdot\!14-10\!\cdot\!39,\;-10\!\cdot\!14+4\!\cdot\!39) =\tfrac1{20}(30,16)=(1.5,\,0.8).

Check against the shortcut: x‾=2.5,y‾=3.5\bar x=2.5,\bar y=3.5, Sxx=5S_{xx}=5, Sxy=4S_{xy}=4, so θ1=4/5=0.8\theta_1=4/5=0.8 and θ0=3.5−0.8(2.5)=1.5\theta_0=3.5-0.8(2.5)=1.5. ✓

(b) Predictions (2.3,3.1,3.9,4.7)(2.3,3.1,3.9,4.7), residuals (0.3,0.1,−1.1,0.7)(0.3,0.1,-1.1,0.7) — note they sum to 00, as Problem 3 requires. Squares sum to 1.801.80, so J(θ⋆)=0.90J(\theta^\star)=0.90.

(c) tr=34\operatorname{tr}=34, det=20\det=20, so λ=34±342−802\lambda=\tfrac{34\pm\sqrt{34^2-80}}2, giving λmax≈33.40\lambda_{\max}\approx33.40 and λmin≈0.599\lambda_{\min}\approx0.599. Hence α<2/33.40≈0.0599\alpha<2/33.40\approx0.0599, and κ≈55.8\kappa\approx55.8 — badly conditioned for such a tiny problem, because xx was never centred.

(d) Step 1: ∇J=X⊤X⋅0−X⊤y→=(−14,−39)\nabla J=X^\top X\cdot0-X^\top\vec y=(-14,-39), so θ1=0.05(14,39)=(0.70,1.95)\theta_1=0.05(14,39)=(0.70,\,1.95) and J=12.82J=12.82.
Step 2: X⊤Xθ1=(22.3,65.5)X^\top X\theta_1=(22.3,\,65.5), so ∇J=(8.3,26.5)\nabla J=(8.3,\,26.5) and θ2=(0.285,0.625)\theta_2=(0.285,\,0.625), J=6.44J=6.44. The overshoot in θ1\theta_1 then correction is the zig-zag of Fig 5 in miniature — α=0.05\alpha=0.05 is stable but close to the 0.05990.0599 limit.

Problem 11 ★★★

Under the model of §8, derive the MLE of σ2\sigma^2. Is it unbiased?

Solution

ℓ(θ,σ)=−mlogσ−m2log2π−12σ2∑i(y(i)−θ⊤x(i))2\ell(\theta,\sigma)=-m\log\sigma-\tfrac m2\log2\pi-\tfrac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_i(y^{(i)}-\theta^\top x^{(i)})^2. With θ̂\hat\theta already fixed, set ∂ℓ/∂σ=0\partial\ell/\partial\sigma=0:

−mσ+1σ3∑iri2=0⇒σ̂2=1m∑i=1mri2=2J(θ̂)m.-\frac m\sigma+\frac1{\sigma^3}\sum_i r_i^2=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat\sigma^2=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m r_i^2=\frac{2J(\hat\theta)}{m}.

It is biased downward. The residuals satisfy n+1n+1 linear constraints (orthogonality to each column of XX), so only m−n−1m-n-1 degrees of freedom remain and 𝔼[σ̂2]=m−n−1mσ2\mathbb{E}[\hat\sigma^2]=\frac{m-n-1}{m}\sigma^2. The unbiased estimator divides by m−n−1m-n-1 instead of mm — the same reason the sample variance uses m−1m-1, which is the special case n=0n=0.

Problem 12 ★★

Derive θ1=Sxy/Sxx\theta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx} and θ0=y‾−θ1x‾\theta_0=\bar y-\theta_1\bar x for the single-feature case directly from the normal equations, where Sxy=∑i(x(i)−x‾)(y(i)−y‾)S_{xy}=\sum_i(x^{(i)}-\bar x)(y^{(i)}-\bar y) and Sxx=∑i(x(i)−x‾)2S_{xx}=\sum_i(x^{(i)}-\bar x)^2.

Solution

Here X⊤X=[m∑x∑x∑x2]X^\top X=\begin{bmatrix}m&\sum x\\\sum x&\sum x^2\end{bmatrix} and X⊤y→=[∑y∑xy]X^\top\vec y=\begin{bmatrix}\sum y\\\sum xy\end{bmatrix}. The first equation is mθ0+θ1∑x=∑ym\theta_0+\theta_1\sum x=\sum y, i.e. θ0=y‾−θ1x‾\theta_0=\bar y-\theta_1\bar x — the fitted line passes through the centroid.

Substituting into the second, θ0∑x+θ1∑x2=∑xy\theta_0\sum x+\theta_1\sum x^2=\sum xy, gives θ1(∑x2−mx‾2)=∑xy−mx‾y‾\theta_1(\sum x^2-m\bar x^2)=\sum xy-m\bar x\bar y. Both sides are the centred sums: ∑x2−mx‾2=Sxx\sum x^2-m\bar x^2=S_{xx} and ∑xy−mx‾y‾=Sxy\sum xy-m\bar x\bar y=S_{xy}. Hence θ1=Sxy/Sxx\theta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}, which you may also read as θ1=r⋅sy/sx\theta_1=r\cdot s_y/s_x — the correlation, rescaled by the two standard deviations.

Problem 13 ★★

Diagnose each, in one line: (a) JJ drops for 20 iterations then rises steadily; (b) JJ drops fast then flattens at 40× the value the closed form gives; (c) SGD's loss bounces between 100 and 140 forever; (d) coefficients are ±107\pm10^7 but predictions look fine; (e) it works on 1,000 rows and overflows on 1,000,000.

Solution
  • (a) α\alpha above 2/λmax2/\lambda_{\max}. The first iterations shrink the well-conditioned directions while the stiffest one is already growing; once it dominates, JJ rises. Reduce α\alpha.
  • (b) Large κ\kappa: the slow eigen-direction has barely moved. Standardise the features, or just use the closed form.
  • (c) The constant-step noise ball (G9), not a bug. Decay α\alpha, or average the last iterates.
  • (d) Collinear features. XθX\theta is well determined even though θ\theta is not (Problem 6). Fine for prediction, meaningless for interpretation; ridge if you need stable coefficients.
  • (e) The sum-convention JJ (G2): the gradient scaled with mm while α\alpha did not. Switch to the mean, or divide α\alpha by mm.

Quick self-check

Ten seconds each. If any answer does not come immediately, the section is named.

Why is x0x_0 defined to be 1?

So the intercept θ0\theta_0 becomes an ordinary weight on an ordinary feature, and no update rule needs a special case for it. (§1)

What is the Hessian of JJ, and why do you care?

X⊤XX^\top X, constant. Positive semidefinite ⇒ JJ convex ⇒ any stationary point is global. Its eigenvalues set both the safe learning rate and the convergence speed. (§3, §4)

Is hθ(x)=θ0+θ1x+θ2x2h_\theta(x)=\theta_0+\theta_1x+\theta_2x^2 linear regression?

Yes. Linear in θ\theta is what matters; x2x^2 is just another fixed feature. (§1, §9)

Give the exact largest safe learning rate.

α<2/λmax(X⊤X)\alpha<2/\lambda_{\max}(X^\top X), with the fastest choice at 2/(λmin+λmax)2/(\lambda_{\min}+\lambda_{\max}). (§4)

Does feature scaling change the fitted model?

No — identical predictions and identical optimal JJ; coefficients transform by 1/σj1/\sigma_j. It changes only the number of iterations. (§4, Problem 5)

Why does SGD work when each step uses the wrong gradient?

Each step is unbiased for 1m∇J\tfrac1m\nabla J; the noise averages out over many steps. (§5)

Will SGD with a fixed α\alpha reach θ⋆\theta^\star?

No. It settles into a noise ball of radius ∝α\propto\alpha. You must decay α\alpha to converge. (§5)

What does X⊤(Xθ−y→)=0X^\top(X\theta-\vec y)=0 mean geometrically?

The residual is orthogonal to the column space of XX, i.e. Xθ⋆X\theta^\star is the orthogonal projection of y→\vec y onto it. (§6)

Two reasons X⊤XX^\top X might not be invertible.

Linearly dependent features, or fewer examples than parameters (m<n+1m<n+1). Fix with lstsq, feature removal, or ridge. (§7)

Why should you never call inv here?

κ(X⊤X)=κ(X)2\kappa(X^\top X)=\kappa(X)^2, so forming the product squares the error amplification. Use a QR/SVD solver on XX itself. (§7)

14 Reference implementation

Every method above, in about 60 lines of NumPy, with a self-check that proves they agree. The full file is attached to the conversation as cs229_lecture2.py.

import numpy as np

def add_intercept(X):                 # the x_0 = 1 convention
    return np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]

def cost(X, y, th):                   # J(theta) = 1/2 ||X th - y||^2
    r = X @ th - y
    return 0.5 * r @ r

def gradient(X, y, th):               # grad J = X^T (X th - y)
    return X.T @ (X @ th - y)

# ---- batch gradient descent -----------------------------------------
def batch_gd(X, y, alpha=None, iters=500, tol=1e-10):
    th = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    if alpha is None:                 # inside 0 < alpha < 2 / lambda_max
        alpha = 1.0 / np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X).max()
    for _ in range(iters):
        g = gradient(X, y, th)
        th -= alpha * g
        if np.linalg.norm(g) < tol:   # gradient-norm stopping rule
            break
    return th

# ---- mini-batch / stochastic gradient descent -----------------------
def sgd(X, y, alpha0, epochs=50, batch=1, decay=True, seed=0):
    rng, m = np.random.default_rng(seed), len(y)
    th, k, t0 = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0, 20.0 * len(y)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for idx in np.array_split(rng.permutation(m), max(1, m // batch)):
            a = alpha0 / (1 + k / t0) if decay else alpha0   # Robbins-Monro
            th -= a * gradient(X[idx], y[idx], th)
            k += 1
    return th

# ---- closed form, three ways ----------------------------------------
def normal_eq_inverse(X, y):          # the textbook formula. do not use.
    return np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y

def normal_eq_solve(X, y):            # Cholesky. better, still kappa(X)^2.
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)

def least_squares_qr(X, y):           # QR/SVD on X itself. use this one.
    return np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]

def ridge(X, y, lam=1.0):             # invertible for any X when lam > 0
    D = np.eye(X.shape[1]); D[0, 0] = 0.0      # never penalise the intercept
    return np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lam * D, X.T @ y)

# ---- the diagnostics you actually reach for when it misbehaves ------
def diagnose(X, y):
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X)
    return {"rank": np.linalg.matrix_rank(X),
            "full column rank": np.linalg.matrix_rank(X) == X.shape[1],
            "lambda_max": ev.max(), "lambda_min": ev.min(),
            "kappa": ev.max() / ev.min() if ev.min() > 0 else np.inf,
            "alpha must satisfy": f"0 < alpha < {2 / ev.max():.3e}",
            "contraction per step": abs(1 - ev.min() / ev.max())}

What the self-check prints

Running the attached file on 400 examples with five deliberately unscaled features reproduces every claim on this page:

  standardised   kappa =    1.363e+00   alpha_max = 4.217e-03   contraction = 0.266234

=== all five solvers on the standardised design ===

  normal eq (solve)    J =     97.70603   max|theta - theta_lstsq| = 2.56e-13

=== SGD: constant step vs Robbins-Monro decay ===

Three lines there are worth staring at. α=1.9/λmax\alpha=1.9/\lambda_{\max} converges and α=2.1/λmax\alpha=2.1/\lambda_{\max} diverges, with marginal oscillation exactly at 22 — the bound in §4 is tight, not conservative. inv raises on the rank-deficient design while lstsq returns the same optimal JJ. And the constant-step SGD floor sits three orders of magnitude above the decayed one, which is G9 in numbers.
